It's a good question: why are the GAAP rules what they are? It needs to be investigated, though.

The reason it happens in multiple quarters is likely that Anthropic's valuation has increased in multiple quarters. Every time Anthropic's valuation increases, the convertible bonds are worth more money. Other shareholders have "lost" money compared to what would have happened if Anthropic had sold regular bonds instead of convertible bonds. Except that no, the value of their shares is increasing too. An increased valuation is actually good for them.

That's how equity works. If someone owns 1% of a company and its valuation doubles, their share is worth twice as much and so is yours and we wouldn't even normally consider it to be diluting the other shareholders.

So the question is whether convertible bonds are worth more than regular bonds and the answer is, yes, absolutely, but they are partially equity, and it's the equity part that's increasing when the company's valuation is increasing.

And if the company's valuation went down then the value of the equity part of the convertible bonds would decrease. Maybe that would be a profit by GAAP rules?

Sometimes accounting is weird because it's necessary to prevent tricks. Why do all your held-to-maturity bonds become "tainted" and get revalued at market prices when you sell a couple, even though nothing has changed about them? Because any other rule would let a company which cannot in fact hold bonds to maturity get up to tricks and systematically overstate their assets.

So while yes, this does look a lot like shareholder dilution, that doesn't really satisfy the question of why it's not treated that way under GAAP. Perhaps GAAP is just wrong, or perhaps there's some possible tricks which Anthropic is provably not engaging in. What it's definitely not is a one-time adjustment now that it's happened in two consecutive quarters.

It’s like shareholder dilution from issuing more stock or stock options. Existing shareholders might have a smaller share of the company than they thought. The accounting is weird.

We aren’t shareholders, though, so why should we care?

FWIW Bitcoin had the same dynamics. Its valuation between 2011-2021 basically derived from a superposition of two futures: one in which it took over the entire global economy and became the dominant reserve currency, and one in which it failed and its value went to zero. The middle-ground was effectively excluded because currencies have strong network effects and a currency that is not dominant within a market quickly ends up unacceptable to merchants and worthless.

It's still somewhat in that grey zone, used as a form of digital gold by people who believe that the dominant reserve currency (USD) is going to zero as well as a trading medium by rogue nations, but its performance has been lackluster since 2021. It's currently up about 20% since then.

Well, it's true that Google has a lab-like structure. Computing the index is a massive continuous "training" job that takes multiple entire clusters (when I worked there at least), and a Google cluster could easily consume an entire rented colo facility. And you need to have crawled large chunks of the web, then done a lot of expensive calculations, before you can serve a single query. So I think the reason for the value gap is purely in the proprietary IP. The recipe for making a good LLM is more or less public, unless you buy into the "everyone just distils claude/gpt" angle. The recipe for making a good search engine is private.

Ultimately it's marginal, meaning that every $ of revenue that Google and Meta make have an associated compute cost with it, but scale your revenue down and you scale compute down also. Moreover this compute cost per revenue is fairly low. A small cloud instance equivalent's of compute can generate a ton of business value.

The big foundational labs are not like this. Every model they release takes a ton of data infrastructure and training (pre, train, post) compute. Then inference itself requires compute. Even if the labs sell tokens, each token embodies a lot of training and inference compute. This is a much more capital heavy business, so I can see revenue multiples being smaller than pure SaaS businesses. A model release bust (like Opus 5) ends up leading to big losses because of the necessary training compute spent on the model and the labor spent on training. A bust SaaS product ends up being wound down quickly, and only costs the labor spent on building it and the compute spent running it.

They reported a loss here because they sold notes convertible into shares and their valuation went up. Normally shareholders do not lose money when the stock price goes up.

It's weird that they had to report it like this because they are technically derivatives, and if they had just given out actual shares (as with stock-based comp), they wouldn't. Yes, giving people stock is a real cost, but what happens to the price afterwards is not, and when the price goes up shareholders are definitely making money, not losing it.

Either way, they did report it. It is up to you to decide how you interpret that information.

Q3 numbers are not what you want to see heading into an IPO.

Again the issue is not is Anthropic an amazing growth story. Zero would debate that.

The issue is this is a probably $200-300B company pretending it’s a $2T company.

Add to that the insane amount of committed spend, a high interest rate environment which means they’ll pay a painful premium to patch cashflow gaps, and a likely “junk” bond rating (per Friday’s news) and that’s why folks are concerned.

It’s also just wrong to keep dismissing the paper losses from convertible notes as somehow not real losses. Once they are a public company this will be actual value taken away from existing public shareholders so they are legit losses not to be ignored. It’s like claiming equity based comp is free money… it’s not, you’re taking it out of the pockets of shareholders.

We desperately need to ground these discussions in actual numbers.

This should help build some intuition and establish a baseline for what the $2T valuation means.

If you buy at $2T Anthropic needs to be worth about $3T by 2030 for a normal market return. That's ~25x P/E and ~$120B/year of profit.

That could be something like $400B of revenue at 30% net margins, $300B at 40%, or $600B at 20%.

It would take 1.7x revenue growth a year to get from today’s $68B run-rate to $400B by 2030. Anthropic's current growth rate is ~4.7x a year. Anthropic doesn't need to maintain that, they basically just need to prevent it from absolutely collapsing and hope margins hold up against open weight models.
